Each agent has its own personality and responsibilities, but they aren’t isolated. They can read shared context, reference each other’s memories, understand how the business works, and operate more like a hive mind than disconnected chatbots.

Slack is the workspace where this comes alive.

Agents can work in channels, escalate issues to each other, hand off tasks, summarize context, ask for help, and report back when something is done. A support issue can turn into an engineering check. A content blocker can turn into a research task. A business question can turn into a coordinated workflow across multiple agents.

Jarvis’s job is to manage that loop.

Instead of me prompting five different agents over and over until something finally gets finished, I can give Jarvis the outcome I want. He routes the work, follows up, checks whether agents are stuck, pushes tasks forward, and brings me the final answer or decision point.

That’s the difference between “chatting with AI” and actually using AI coworkers.

I’m not trying to replace human creativity. I’m trying to build an operating system for getting work done: faster, more consistently, and with fewer dropped balls.
